subject: Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local

messages.author: 74170f154580ff51
messages.subject: Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local
parts:
Dear all,

I am new to Stan and am trying to fit a simple hierarchical model: Basically I model the observed number of ticks where z is the "true" number of ticks, with p modelling the observation error (undercounting).

data {
    int<lower=1> N; // sample size
    int<lower=0> ticks[N]; // number of ticks per sheep
}
parameters {
    vector<lower=0>[N] lambda;

    real<lower=0> alpha;
    real<lower=0> upsilon;
    real<lower=0, upper=1> p;

}
model {
   
    int z[N];

    p ~ beta(14.64, 168.36);
    alpha ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
    upsilon ~ gamma(0.1, 0.1);
    lambda ~ gamma(alpha, upsilon);

    z ~ poisson(lambda);
    ticks ~ binomial(z, 1 - p);

}

When I try to fit the model, Stan complains:

> m3 <- stan('ticks_hierarchical_sampling_error.stan',
+     data=data, iter = 1000, chains = 4)
DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
Warning (non-fatal):
Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
If it does, you need to include a target += statement with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
Left-hand-side of sampling statement:
    z ~ poisson(...)

What does that mean?

Thank you very much!
Adrian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local
parts:
I'm afraid you can't actually code that model in Stan if I understand
your intent to make z work like a parameter. You can code many related
models in Stan, but not models with latent count variables. For example,
you could do something like this:

ticks ~ poisson((1 - p) * lambda);

but you're going to find that hard to fit because you have a different lambda
for each tick value and so lambda[n] is just going to be driven to
ticks / (1 - p).

Stan's sampling statement only increments the log density, so that
program's not going to do what you think. This confusion among users
is why we may wind up getting rid of "~" altogether in the future. We've
tried to call this out clearly to the point of rearranging the user
manual to put it front and center, but it's a persistent source of
queries to this list.

Before you call y ~ foo(theta), both y and theta need to be defined (not
just declared). The default initialization for an integer is the smallest
negative number (-2^31 or thereabouts). So what you're saying in that loop
is equivalent to:

for (n in 1:N)
-2^31 ~ poisson(...);

which is presumably not what you want. For a start, Poisson requires
positive variates. So Stan should completely bomb out when you try to
run this model, not just when you compile it.

You could define your model in BUGS or JAGS (or even in PyMC3).
But for what it's worth, in BUGS and JAGS, the sampling statements
don't sample---they just construct a graphical model that's then
sampled using Gibbs, not literally by drawing the left hand side from
the right hand side of a ~.

- Bob
